title: Shiraz and Isfahan, 1409-14: the second prince
dramatic_question: Iskandar Mīrzā wants you at his court too. How much of what he offers do you take?

situation.when: 812-17/1409-14 (Melvin-Koushki's own dates for this court disagree; see the first item below)

invariants.text: Iskandar Mīrzā took his brother's place in Shiraz and soon afterwards set up a brilliant court in Isfahan.
invariants.detail: Melvin-Koushki's timeline is not consistent about when: one line has you a member of Iskandar's court in Isfahan from 812-15/1409-12, another has Iskandar taking Isfahan and founding that court only in 815-17/1412-14.

invariants.text: Iskandar too made you a member of his court and gave you similar honours. This comes from your second apology, written to Bāysunghur while your own case was unresolved; Melvin-Koushki reports it.
Melvin-Koushki says the Timurid elite, and in particular Iskandar and later Bāysunghur, showed obvious interest in your lettrist doctrine.

prose: You served one grandson of Temür; now you serve his brother. Iskandar Mīrzā takes Pīr-Muḥammad's place at Shiraz and, soon after, builds a court at Isfahan that Melvin-Koushki calls brilliant.

Melvin-Koushki reads Iskandar as an overt Shiʿi, or at least a devoted lover of the Imams, with a pronounced interest in lettrism (following Aubin). That is a scholar's reading of Iskandar's patronage, not something you are recorded saying. It leaves open who led whom: his later papers do not agree on whether Iskandar took up lettrism at your instance or commissioned you.
The record says you were given honours. It does not say which. Melvin-Koushki presumes a teaching post and a judgeship and puts a question mark beside it in his own timeline.

choices.label: Join Iskandar's court and accept the honours he gives, as you did under his brother.
choices.feedback: This is what your second apology says, as Melvin-Koushki reports it: Iskandar made you a member of his court with similar honours. Note whose word it is: a plea to Bāysunghur in 1431-32, so it shows what you told him, not everything that happened. Melvin-Koushki thinks it not unlikely that this attachment was later seen as a liability (his own causal reading, not a fact in the sources); that is why your exposure rises.

choices.label: Take the teaching post and judgeship Melvin-Koushki presumes, and sit among the scholars the prince gathers.
choices.feedback: This is a scholar's proposal, not a record. The post and judgeship are 'presumably' Melvin-Koushki's, with a '(?)' in his timeline. That you met the astronomers Ghiyās al-Dīn and Maḥmūd Kāshī, the poets Busḥāq Aṭʿima and Mīr Ḥaydar and the historian Muʿīn al-Dīn Naṭanzī is 'would have', from Soucek. The game lets you take it and charges you for it in exposure; it does not treat it as fact.

choices.label: Decline the honours and go on teaching on your own, outside Iskandar's court.
choices.feedback: The sources put you inside this court, and Melvin-Koushki reads Iskandar as your patron in Shiraz and Isfahan until Shāhrukh's campaign of 817/1414, from your letters. Nobody records you refusing him. The game returns you to the record. What you gained and paid here stays in your ledger; the story then rejoins the record.
costs: You keep your students and stay clear of a court that may later count against you, so exposure falls. You lose the honours and the income that came with them.
